metadata.title: Shaders in 3D
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: What changes when a shader goes three-D
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); a shader from a small game; see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Shaders in three D. Learn what changes when a shader draws a three-D surface, how lighting and the renderer change the color you get, and how to read a real one.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Many people think a three-D shader is a different, harder thing. It is not. It has the same shape as a two-D shader, with new names and one new idea: light.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A mesh is the points and triangles that make a three-D shape. A material tells Godot how to draw a surface. Albedo is the base color of a surface. Lighting is how lights change that color. A renderer is the part of Godot that draws the picture.

terms.meaning: the set of vertices and triangles that make a shape
the resource that tells Godot how to draw a surface; it holds the shader
the base color of a surface
how lights change a surface's color
the part of Godot that draws

beats.narration_text: A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. In two-D or three-D, it has the same shape: a first line, up to three functions, and dials your game can turn.

shot.visual_intent: The compiled skeleton file lab-shaders/03-skeleton-3d.gdshader drawn as a cream code card (Menlo, 12 lines). Brackets draw in on the voice's words and each carries a one-word label: 'a first line' brackets line 1 (label 'type'), 'up to three functions' brackets lines 5 to 12, the three empty functions (label 'functions'), 'dials' brackets line 3 where a small dial (a circle with a turning tick) sits at the card's right (label 'dials'). Caption at the top, GLOSSARY wording: 'shader: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn'.

show.event: card and shader caption; a terracotta dot steps down the lines like a program counter

shot.motion_claim: A dot steps down the lines like a program, then three brackets draw in one after another, each with its label, and a small dial turns.

beats.narration_text: The first line says what the shader is for. Canvas item means two-D. Spatial means three-D, where the shader draws a mesh: the points and triangles that make a shape.

shot.visual_intent: The line `shader_type canvas_item;` in Menlo over a flat teal square (outline icon). On the cue the word canvas_item slides out and spatial slides in, while the flat square turns into an isometric cube in the same teal with faint triangle edges; a one-word label 'mesh' points at the cube. Caption, GLOSSARY wording: 'shader type: the first line; says what the shader is for'.

shot.motion_claim: The word canvas_item is replaced by spatial and the flat square turns into a cube.

lecture.why: Two worlds, each with its own first line, is the contrast the sentence names; a replaced word plus a square that becomes a cube says it with motion.

beats.narration_text: Both types use the same three functions. Vertex runs once for each vertex, a corner point of the mesh. A flat square has four. Fragment runs once for each pixel the mesh covers. Light runs once per pixel, for every light.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the test rectangle (a flat square) with four terracotta corner dots. Right: a 12-by-8 pixel grid of outline cells with the square's footprint over it. The four dots flash in order with a counter 1 to 4 and the label 'vertex()'; the covered cells tint one by one, each with a tiny 'fragment()' tag, then all hold; a small lamp icon (drawn bulb with rays) appears and the covered cells brighten once per lamp, two lamps in turn, with the label 'light()'. Captions, GLOSSARY wording: 'vertex: a corner point of a shape' and 'pixel: one dot of the picture on screen'.

show.event: square with four dots; both captions
covered cells tint one by one
lamp 1 then lamp 2 brighten the cells

shot.motion_claim: Four dots flash in turn, then the covered cells tint one by one, then the cells brighten once for each lamp.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: 'Once for each vertex', 'once for each pixel' and 'once per light' are counts; four dots, a tinting grid and two lamps are those counts as motion.

beats.narration_text: The other change is the output. A two-D shader sets color: four numbers, red, green, blue and alpha. A three-D shader sets albedo: three numbers. Alpha becomes a separate output.

shot.visual_intent: Two code cards, lab-shaders/01-flat-teal-2d.gdshader at left and lab-shaders/02-flat-teal-3d.gdshader at right (Menlo, 5 lines each), the same positions line for line. The first lines already differ (canvas_item and spatial: label 'type', the idea of the previous beat). On the cues the changed pieces get a terracotta ring in turn: 'COLOR' becomes 'ALBEDO' as the voice says 'the output' (label 'output'); a short ring goes round the four numbers of the two-D color as the voice says 'four numbers'; as it says 'and alpha' the ring moves to the last number, 1.0, and a caption lands, GLOSSARY wording: 'alpha: how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid'; as it says 'three numbers' 'vec4(' becomes 'vec3(' and ', 1.0' dissolves (label 'three numbers'); as it says 'Alpha becomes a separate output' a small 'ALPHA' chip appears beside the card. The unchanged text stays still.

beats.narration_text: Get either one wrong and Godot says so. Write color in a three-D shader and it answers: constants cannot be modified. Color exists there, but you can only read it. Give albedo four numbers and it answers: invalid arguments, vec three, vec four.

shot.visual_intent: A plain terminal window (CCPlainShell, 32 pt) with two real runs, verbatim from the Lab's log. Each run is a comment line with the line that was wrong, then the compiler's two output lines. A terracotta ring (grey-backed) rings each 'SHADER ERROR' line as the voice reads the message. Title: 'Godot 4.7.2 · what the compiler says'. Line cues are frames at 24 fps and are approximate: re-time them to the measured audio.

beats.narration_text: Some mix-ups are silent. Give a three-D mesh a two-D shader, and the running game raises no error. It draws the mesh as if it had no shader at all. When a shader seems ignored, check the first line.

Real Godot render: two flat squares side by side, both plain grey at first. At the hand-over (0.12 of the clip, as the voice says 'Give a three-D mesh a two-D shader') each is given a red shader: the left one gets the canvas_item shader above, the right one a spatial shader that paints red. The right square turns red; the left stays exactly as it was. Labels land under them: 'canvas_item: ignored' and 'spatial: red'.

beats.narration_text: U V is a point's address on the shape: zero to one across, zero to one down. Paint it as a color, red across and green down. A square, a box and a sphere each show a different map, because the mesh supplies the address.

shot.visual_intent: A wide result strip (layout 'stack': result above, and under it a one-line excerpt: line 5 of the six-line shader, `ALBEDO = vec3(UV.x, UV.y, 0.0);`, with a tag 'red = UV.x (across), green = UV.y (down)'). Real Godot render: a flat square, a box and a sphere in a row, all swinging side to side about the vertical axis (plus or minus 50 degrees, one swing in eight seconds), every one painted with red-across, green-down address colors. The square shows the whole red-green gradient, the box shows a different patch on each face, the sphere wraps its map around itself. One-word labels land under them: 'square', 'box', 'sphere'. Caption, GLOSSARY wording: 'UV: a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'.

beats.narration_text: To use a shader, give the mesh instance a shader material. In three-D that slot is called material override. The node holds the material. The material holds your shader.

shot.visual_intent: Three boxes slide in left to right and link: a cube icon over 'mesh instance', then 'ShaderMaterial', then 'shader' (a small file icon marked .gdshader). The link between the first two carries a small tab 'material override'. A dot travels from the shader back to the mesh instance (meaning: look here). Captions: 'mesh instance: the node that draws a mesh' (docs: MeshInstance3D is the main node that draws a mesh) and, GLOSSARY wording, 'ShaderMaterial: a material that holds your shader and its settings'.

beats.narration_text: Now run the one-line albedo shader on a sphere. You wrote one flat teal, so you might expect a flat teal disc. Instead one side is bright and one is dim. You wrote no lighting rule. Godot lit the sphere with the scene's lamp.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the five-line shader (ALBEDO = vec3(0.37, 0.64, 0.57)) with its ALBEDO line focused. Right: a real Godot render of one teal sphere, centred. At first the lamp is off and the sphere is a flat dim disc (the 'flat teal disc' the voice says you might expect). At the reveal the lamp switches on, from the upper left: bright on one side, dim on the other, and it stays that way. Labels land on the sphere: 'bright', then 'dim'; a 'lamp' tag lands in the upper left as the voice names the scene's lamp.

beats.narration_text: In three-D, the fragment function describes a surface. Albedo is its base color. Alpha is how visible it is. Emission is light it gives off. Roughness and metallic describe its finish.

shot.visual_intent: A four-row table on the cream stage, one row ringed as each output is named: ALBEDO, ALPHA, EMISSION and ROUGHNESS with METALLIC (the last two share a row), each with a short plain meaning. The note names the docs page.

props.title: What fragment sets in 3D
props.note: Godot 4.7 spatial shader reference · fragment built-ins

shot.motion_claim: The ring steps down the four rows with the voice.

lecture.runner_up: four spheres, one output changing on each
lecture.why: A table of kinds is the right shape for five parallel names; the sphere row was tried and METALLIC = 1 reads near-black without an environment to reflect, which would teach the wrong thing (verify6-outputs.gd).

beats.narration_text: Then Godot's own lighting turns that description, and every lamp, into the pixel you see. You describe the surface. Godot does the lighting. Your color is an input, not the answer.

shot.visual_intent: A left-to-right flow on the cream stage. A box 'fragment()' emits a small card of five monospace chips (ALBEDO, ALPHA, EMISSION, ROUGHNESS, METALLIC) labelled 'surface'. The card travels into a box 'Godot's lighting'. Two lamp icons drop beams into the same box from above. A single teal pixel (a small outlined square) comes out on the right. All arrows are drawn shapes that point only forward.

beats.narration_text: Sometimes you want no lighting. Add a second line: render mode unshaded. Now the result is only albedo, and the lamp is ignored. Watch the lit sphere beside it.

beats.narration_text: Why choose unshaded? No lamp can change the color, so a flat, graphic look stays flat. Godot's docs add that skipping the lighting makes the surface faster to render.

beats.narration_text: You can write the light function yourself. Then your function replaces Godot's lighting for that surface. An empty one is a trap: the lamp stops working. The sphere stays dim, whatever the lamp does.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the eight-line shader with its empty `void light() { }` focused and tagged (GLOSSARY wording: 'light(): runs once per pixel for each light that touches it', then 'replaces the default lighting, even when empty'). Right: a real render of three spheres under the same turning lamp: lit (changing), unshaded (flat) and the one with the empty light() function: it stays dim and flat, ignoring the lamp. Labels: 'lit', 'unshaded', 'own light()'.

beats.narration_text: Another trap. A three-D surface has two sides, and by default only the front is drawn. Turn a flat square around and it vanishes. Add cull disabled to the render mode line, and both sides draw.

Right: a real render of two flat teal squares turning once about the vertical axis: the left one (default culling) blinks out while its back faces the camera, the right one (cull disabled) is always there. Labels: 'default', 'cull disabled'.

beats.narration_text: So when a three-D shader looks wrong, ask two quick questions. Is a lamp changing my color? Add unshaded and see. Is the back side being skipped? Add cull disabled and see. Godot's docs list many more modes, such as blend add.

shot.visual_intent: A small decision sketch. At the top a teal square labelled 'looks wrong'. Two branches go down. Left: a lamp icon with a question mark leads to a shaded sphere that turns flat, tagged 'add unshaded'. Right: a flat square seen from behind (empty outline) leads to the same square filled, tagged 'add cull disabled'. A dot travels down each branch in turn; a third tag 'blend add' appears faint at the side with the caption 'more modes in the docs'.

beats.narration_text: Now build a surface that changes. Start from a picture you already know: the address as a color. On a flat square, the corners read dark, red, green and yellow. The top left is zero, zero.

Right: a real Godot render of a flat square, red across and green down. Corner labels land in the order the voice says them: 'dark' (top left), 'red' (top right), 'green' (bottom left), 'yellow' (bottom right).

lecture.why: The picture itself is the evidence that the address became a color, and the corners prove the orientation (top left is zero, zero).

(The Lab's own quad3d fills the whole 16:9 frame: a wide rectangle, not the square the voice says.) Corner probes (0.02/0.98 of the quad): dark (0.149, 0.157, 0), red (0.992, 0.157, 0), green (0.149, 0.988, 0), yellow (0.992, 0.988, 0).

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A three-D shader has the same shape as a two-D one, with new names. Albedo is the base color, and the address comes from the mesh. Surfaces are lit by default, and unshaded gives you the albedo with no lamp. Fract, step and mix cut stripes and blend colors, and a uniform lets the game steer. The pad is ten lines: a type, a mode, three dials, a stripe, a base and a blend. A pixel is true for one renderer, so name it when you test.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot spatial shader for a mesh instance, with render mode unshaded. Give it one float uniform called charge, from zero to one, and two color uniforms marked source color. Paint eight stripes in the first color using step and fract on the U V address, and mix toward a plain second color as charge rises. Then tell me which renderer your colors assume. Then check two things yourself. At charge one, are the stripes gone? And when you switch the renderer, does the half-charge color change?
